The smell from fermentation always seems to be trapped in the bottle and ruin the cider, at least for months. What am I doing wrong? I've given up so far, and waiting for a kegerator.
Anyone have real success with bottle priming?

Well, kegerators are great. I use a chest freezer, then attach a regulator on it to keep it at desired temp. Plus, it's easier to load, clean and can hold more kegs. I keep one dedicated to cider. Well, not this year. Too busy distilling for a living to keep up on the homebrewing like I should.

That said, bottle priming is a pain. Are you doing a secondary fermentation? Are you waiting until the cider goes clear? What's the specific gravity of it?

Also, what kind of smell are you getting? If it has a "sour" yeasty smell, it may actually be from an infection instead of from the yeast.

I stop it at 1.000 and the cider is usually clear. There is no sulfur smell before I bottle it, only afterwords. I've been using apple juice concentrate and brown sugar to backsweeten so perhaps the yeast doesn't like that sugar. I've thought about adding yeast nutrient again after fermentation so the yeast isn't stressed during bottle priming.

The key, if you don't mind me being a busy body, is to get as much dead yeast out of solution as possible. You don't need much C02 to carbonate inside the bottle.

After initial fermentation, I would rack the cider into another vessel for a few weeks to let the yeast settle off the traub. Then rack it again into a third vessel that will act as your bottling bucket. Fill from that.

Also, you mentioned a sulfur smell. Now normally you get that from lager yeast instead of ale yeast (also from too farm a ferment). You might want to switch strains and have a little more temp control, not only during ferment but during bottle conditioning.

What do you mean by "the smell from fermentation"?

Are you getting a sulfury odor? If so, don't bottle until it goes away!

I have had success with bottle priming, but I much prefer my cider at least off dry and potentially even semi sweet--so I generally just keg and backsweeten at kegging.

You can backsweeten at bottling, but you'll need to keep a close eye on carb levels and either pasteurize or just fridge (and keep fridged) the whole batch as soon as the carb level is where you want it (and probably actually a little before if you're fridging the batch).

There is no sulfur smell before I bottle it, only afterwords. I've been using apple juice concentrate and brown sugar to backsweeten so perhaps the yeast doesn't like that sugar. I've thought about adding yeast nutrient again after fermentation so the yeast isn't stressed during bottle priming.

Try just plain sugar (cane or corn) for bottle carbing. If you're not pasteurizing or fridging the whole batch when it gets to a carb level you like, skip backsweetening in the bottle.

Instead, add some fresh apple juice, simple syrup or concentrate to your glass at serving. :)

When you're talking about allergies, or even something like snake venom; in most cases multiple exposures to it create an immunity in the person. I know I've been bitten by mosquitoes countless times, and everyone else probably has a well. Why do we still have a reaction to the bite?
Why don't we develop an immunity to mosquito bites?

The kind of developed immunity to which you are referring is known as Immunological memory, which is the bodies ability to recognize pathogens by their antigens and dispatch them with the same antibodies that the body used during a previous invasion of the same pathogen. This is why, for instance, people who suffered from measles or chicken pox as a child are now immune from them, because their body fought it off once and now knows the weapons that are super effective against it.

For millenia, humans have been subjecting themselves to diluted snake venom repeatedly in order to develop an immunity to them, a process similar to vaccination. More recently, a man named Bill Haast had "injected himself with snake venom during most of his adult life, in an effort to build up an immunity to a broad array of venomous snakes ... Haast lived to age 100, and survived a reported 172 snake bites. He donated his blood to be used in treating snake-bite victims when a suitable anti-venom was not available. More than twenty of those individuals recovered."

As for why this doesn't happen with mosquito bites, when a mosquito bites you, after it saws around to find a blood vessel, it releases an anticoagulant to keep your blood from clotting so it can feast. The actual bumpy, itchy bite you see and feel after the mosqutio leaves is your body's response to this anticoagulant. This infographic visualizes this process well.

TL;DR: Snake venom and other diseases are targeted by the immune system, and thus have an immunity developed against them, while mosquitoes use no such venom, so its not the antibodies' problem.
